verses.translation_literal: And it was at that time, and Judah went down from with his brothers, and he turned aside to a man, an Adullamite, and his name [was] Hirah.
verses.translation_dramatic: In those days Judah left. He walked down out of his father's hill country, away from his brothers, and left their company behind him like a closed door. Where the road bent, he turned aside and stopped at the tents of a man of Adullam, a man called Hirah.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is a departure, and the verbs say so: 'went down' (וַיֵּרֶד) is the same verb the narrative has just used for Joseph being taken down to Egypt, and the chapter begins by sending a second son of Jacob downhill. Radak and the midrash he cites read it morally: Judah is brought down from his standing among his brothers. Radak also gives a plain geographic reading, since Adullam lies down in the lowland. The KJV's 'turned in to' is archaic and blunts a verb that means 'to pitch aside, to turn off the road' (וַיֵּט, from the root for pitching a tent, which Radak reads literally as Judah pitching his tent), and 'a certain Adullamite' smooths the Hebrew's blunt 'a man, an Adullamite'. Note 'from with his brothers' (מֵאֵת אֶחָיו): he takes himself out of their company, not just away from a place. Actors: this is a man who has just helped to sell his brother, and who now goes to live among others.

philological_notes.note: 'Went down.' The same verb that frames Joseph's descent to Egypt in the preceding chapters; here the descent is Judah's own, away from his brothers and toward the lowland of Adullam. Radak reads it both geographically and as moral decline.

'Turned aside,' literally to stretch out or pitch aside; Radak understands that Judah pitched his tent with his flock and joined himself to this man. The KJV's 'turned in to' conveys direction but not the settling.

verses.translation_literal: And Judah saw there a daughter of a man, a Canaanite, and his name [was] Shua, and he took her and he went in to her.
verses.translation_dramatic: And there Judah saw her: the daughter of a Canaanite, a man by the name of Shua. He took her, and he went in to her.
verses.directors_commentary: Three quick verbs, 'saw, took, went in', carry the whole courtship. There is no betrothal speech, no father's blessing, no bridal gift reported; the narrator moves at Judah's own pace, and Radak reads 'saw' as desire: she pleased him. Radak adds that 'took her' means he took her as a wife first and went in afterward, so this is marriage and not a liaison. The KJV 'a certain Canaanite' invents a phrase the Hebrew lacks and 'went in unto her' is already a euphemism for sex, softer than it sounds in English. What matters here: the woman is nameless, identified only through her father, and the father is called 'Canaanite' (כנעני). Onkelos, Rashi, Rashbam, Ibn Ezra, Ramban and Radak all report the Aramaic rendering 'merchant', because the word can mean trader (cf. Hos 12:8, which Rashbam and Ibn Ezra cite); Ramban and Radak add that Jacob's family avoided Canaanite marriages, so the merchant reading removes the problem. I keep the plain gentilic and flag the alternative: a first audience would hear a local, non-family marriage.

philological_notes.note: 'Canaanite,' but the Targum and the medieval commentators also read it as 'merchant' (cf. Hos 12:8), softening the problem of a Canaanite marriage. The verse itself does not decide.
'He went in to her,' the standard Hebrew euphemism for sexual union. Radak stresses the order: first 'took' (marriage), then 'went in'.

verses.translation_literal: And she conceived and she bore a son, and he called his name Er.
verses.translation_dramatic: She conceived, and she bore a son, and Judah named him Er.
verses.directors_commentary: A plain birth notice, and the grammar of naming is the point. Here the father names the child ('and he called'); in the next two verses the mother does ('and she called'). Radak reads this as the household custom: the father names the first, the mother the second. The name Er (עֵר) is not explained by the text; Ramban links it to 'awake, rouse' (the root of 'Awake, O arm of the LORD'), while Genesis Rabbah plays on its sense of being roused out of the world, but the midrash is a reading backward from the fate, not Judah's intention. The KJV 'bare' is archaic for 'bore'. Pace this beat quickly: births stack up like seasons.

philological_notes.note: The name is not explained in the verse. Ramban connects it to the root 'to awaken'; the midrash he reports reads it as 'one who was uprooted from the world', an after-the-fact etymology.

verses.translation_literal: And she conceived again and she bore a son, and she called his name Onan.
verses.translation_dramatic: Again she conceived, and again she bore a son, and this time she named him: Onan.
verses.directors_commentary: The only variation in the birth formula is the subject of the naming: in v.3 Judah 'called' the name, here 'she called' (וַתִּקְרָא). Radak takes this as household custom, the father naming the first son and the mother the second; Ramban reports that view in his comment on 38:5 and rejects it as having 'neither taste nor scent', so treat it as one reader's guess. The text itself gives no reason for either name. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan adds one for Onan: his father was destined to mourn over him. That is the Targum's reading, a name heard backward from the fate, and not a statement of the verse. The KJV 'bare' is archaic for 'bore', but its 'conceived again, and bare a son' is accurate. For actors: the formula is flat and fast, and the repetition (conceive, bear, call) should sound like years going by. Nothing here prepares the audience for what Onan will be.

philological_notes.note: 'And she called' (feminine), against v.3's masculine 'he called'. Radak reads the shift as custom (father names the first son, mother the second); Ramban, reporting this on 38:5, rejects it as without 'taste or scent'. The verse itself offers no reason.
sources: Radak, as reported in Ramban on Genesis 38:5

philological_notes.note: The name is not explained in the verse. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan glosses it with the thought that his father was destined to mourn over him, an after-the-fact reading of the name.

verses.translation_literal: And she added again and she bore a son, and she called his name Shelah. And he was in Kezib when she bore him.
verses.translation_dramatic: A third time she carried, a third time she bore a son, and she called him Shelah. He was at Kezib when she bore him.
verses.directors_commentary: 'She added' (וַתֹּסֶף) is the idiom for 'did it again,' and the KJV's 'yet again conceived' misplaces the weight: the Hebrew says she added to bearing, not that she conceived once more. The closing clause is a riddle: 'and he was in Kezib when she bore him.' Who was in Kezib? The subject is ambiguous. Rashbam and the commentary tradition take it as Judah, away from home at the birth, which Radak reads as the reason the mother, not the father, named the child; Ramban rejects that as without 'taste or scent.' Rashi hears a pun: Kezib (כזיב) sounds like the root of 'deceive, fail' (cf. Jer 15:18), because she stopped bearing. Sforno hears it in Shelah's name too. Treat it as a quiet bad omen: the third son's birthplace is named 'Disappointment.' The place is the Judean town Achzib of Mic 1:14.

philological_notes.note: 'In Kezib,' a town in the Judean lowland. The name sounds like the root meaning 'to lie, to fail'; Rashi hears a wordplay, though Ramban questions why the place would be so named for this event.
Name not explained in the text. Ramban and Sforno link it to a root of deception or neglect ('do not mislead me', 2 Kgs 4:28), echoing Kezib's sense. This is a reading, not a stated meaning.

verses.translation_literal: And Judah took a wife for Er his firstborn, and her name [was] Tamar.
verses.translation_dramatic: In time Judah chose a wife for Er, his firstborn. Her name was Tamar.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a father's act: in the ancient Near East, marriage was a contract between households, and 'Judah took a wife for Er' is exactly how it was done. The son has no verb in this sentence; he is the object of his father's decision. The KJV's 'whose name was Tamar' is fine but the Hebrew arrives with a cold economy: just the name, no father, no origin. The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan adds that she was a daughter of Shem; that is Targum, not text. Tamar means 'date palm', a tree that fruits late and lives long. Play the name lightly: at the first mention it is only a name.

philological_notes.note: A woman's name, also the word for the date palm. Her origin is not given; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan calls her a daughter of Shem, which is its own addition.

verses.translation_literal: And Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil in the eyes of YHWH, and YHWH caused him to die.
verses.translation_dramatic: But Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil in the eyes of the LORD. And the LORD put him to death.
verses.directors_commentary: Two clauses, one verdict, and the divine name is repeated at both ends like a frame: YHWH sees, YHWH acts. The text never says what Er did. Radak says his evil was known to YHWH alone, a matter between him and Tamar; the sages he cites (Yevamot 34) say he deliberately kept her from conceiving, so as not to spoil her beauty, and Rashi, Rashbam and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan follow that line. Ramban notes that the Torah's silence is deliberate and that the death is Er's own, not Judah's punishment for selling Joseph. The KJV 'wicked' (a moral label) and 'slew' (a violent verb) overstate: 'evil' is the same plain word as 'bad' and the verb is simply 'caused to die' (Hiphil). Directors: do not stage a murder. A young man is dead, and the narrator wants the reader to ask why.

philological_notes.note: 'Evil in the eyes of YHWH,' a formula of judgment. The offense is not named. The traditional answer is that he refused to give Tamar a child, but the verse does not say it.
Hiphil, 'caused him to die.' It names YHWH as the agent without describing how, which is why 'slew' in the KJV adds violence the Hebrew lacks.

token_glosses.gloss: and he caused to die him

verses.translation_literal: And Judah said to Onan, "Go in to the wife of your brother, and perform the duty of a husband's brother with her, and raise up offspring for your brother."
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Judah spoke to Onan. "Go in to your brother's wife. Do for her what a brother must do, and raise up a seed for your brother."
verses.directors_commentary: Judah's order is the first appearance in the Bible of what Deuteronomy 25:5–10 later calls levirate duty, and the text treats it as already known: Radak concludes that the custom predates the giving of the Torah. The Hebrew verb is unusual. 'Perform the duty of a husband's brother' (וְיַבֵּם) is built on the noun 'husband's brother' (יָבָם); English has no equivalent verb, so the KJV's 'marry her' is imprecise, since the duty is to father a child, not to take a wife. The goal is stated in the last clause: 'raise up seed for your brother' (וְהָקֵם זֶרַע), meaning preserve his line and name. Rashi reads that the child would be called by the dead man's name; Ramban disputes it, citing Ruth, where Boaz's son is named Obed and not Mahlon. Stakes for actors: an heir is a man's immortality and, for the family, land. Onan stands to inherit the firstborn's share if there is no child.

philological_notes.note: Denominative verb from yavam, 'husband's brother': 'perform the husband's-brother duty.' It names the levirate obligation (cf. Deut 25:5, which Ibn Ezra defers to).

'And raise up seed' (offspring). The purpose of the duty: a child who continues the dead brother's line. Rashi says the child bears the dead man's name; Ramban objects that Ruth 4 contradicts a strict naming rule.

token_glosses.gloss: and perform the husband's-brother duty with

verses.translation_literal: And Onan knew that the offspring would not be his, and it was, if he went in to the wife of his brother, that he spoiled [it] to the ground, so as not to give offspring to his brother.
verses.translation_dramatic: Onan knew that the child would not be his. And so, each time he went in to his brother's wife, he let it spoil on the ground, so that he would give his brother no child.
verses.directors_commentary: Onan's knowledge is the hinge: 'he knew that the seed would not be his' (לֹא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע). Ibn Ezra reads it as 'would not be called by his name', pointing to Deuteronomy 25:6, and both Targums say the same (Onkelos: the seed is not called by his name; Pseudo-Jonathan: the children were not called by his name). The verse does not say what Onan stood to lose. It is a plausible inference, not stated by the verse or by these commentators, that a child counted as his brother's would cost him something in family standing or inheritance; do not play that as fact. Sforno gives a different motive: the brother, not Onan, would gain the merit of the act. The act itself is a euphemism: 'spoiled to the ground' (וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה). Rashi, quoting Genesis Rabbah, says 'threshing within and winnowing without'; Radak says he spoiled his seed to the ground, as was said of Er. Ibn Ezra reports and rejects Ben Tamim's reading that Onan acted against the woman, and calls it madness. The Hebrew is habitual ('it was, if he went in…'): repeated, not a single lapse. The KJV 'spilled it on the ground' supplies an object the Hebrew lacks, and turns 'if' into 'when'; the literal layer brackets the 'it'. For actors: this is calculation, repeated, and Tamar bears the cost.

philological_notes.note: 'The offspring would not be his.' Ibn Ezra explains it as 'would not be called by his name', citing Deut 25:6, and both Targums say the seed would not be called by his name. The verse does not state a further motive.

'And he spoiled/ruined to the ground.' A deliberate indirection: the verb 'to ruin' with 'to the earth' and no stated object. The classical reading is withdrawal before ejaculation. Ibn Ezra reports Ben Tamim's different reading and rejects it.
'If/whenever he went in'; with the preceding 'and it was' it marks repeated action, not a single occasion.

verses.translation_literal: And what he did was evil in the eyes of YHWH, and he caused him to die also.
verses.translation_dramatic: What he had done was evil in the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD put him, too, to death.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse echoes verse 7 on purpose: the same word, 'evil,' the same eyes of YHWH, the same verb of causing death, and 'also' (גַּם) joins the brothers. Rashi and Radak both read it as the same sin and the same death. The KJV 'displeased the Lord' is far softer than the Hebrew, which uses the root 'evil' (וַיֵּרַע): it was evil in His eyes, and the KJV's 'wherefore' invents a causal link the Hebrew gives only as sequence ('and'). Rashbam adds that the sages saw the sin as the destruction of seed to preserve her beauty. Mind the shape: two sons dead in the space of two verses, and the narrator turns away to Judah, who now has a widow in the house.

philological_notes.note: 'And it was evil,' a verb form of the root 'evil/bad.' The KJV 'displeased' is weaker than the Hebrew's moral judgement.
'Him also.' Radak understands it as both brothers dying for one and the same sin.

verses.translation_literal: And Judah said to Tamar his daughter-in-law, "Remain a widow [in] the house of your father until Shelah my son grows up," for he said, "Lest he die also, like his brothers." And Tamar went and she dwelt [in] the house of her father.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Judah said to Tamar, his daughter-in-law, "Go and live as a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah is grown." For he thought: lest he die too, like his brothers. And Tamar went, and she lived in her father's house.
verses.directors_commentary: Judah offers a deferral, and the narrator immediately gives his stated fear: 'for he said, lest he too die like his brothers.' Rashi, citing Ketubot 43, reads it as a presumption that a woman whose husbands die will bury more, and takes the deferral as putting her off with a straw: Judah never meant to give her to Shelah. That is Rashi's reading. Ramban quotes it and rejects it: he asks why Judah would deceive her, and holds that Judah really meant to wait because Shelah was still a boy, too young to risk, and would give her to him once he was grown and heeded his father. Radak, citing Genesis Rabbah (Rabbi Eleazar), says that even where there is no augury there is a sign. Sforno reads 'remain a widow' as 'wait', comparing Hosea 3:3. The KJV 'peradventure' is not in the Hebrew; פֶּן expresses fear, 'lest'. 'Remain a widow' keeps the sense. Practical world: a childless widow went back to her father's house while the levirate duty stayed open; 'widow' (אַלְמָנָה) is a status, neither free to remarry elsewhere nor provided for. Note how quietly Tamar obeys: 'And Tamar went.' For actors, the audience should not know yet whether Judah is lying.

philological_notes.note: 'Widow' as a social status, here the one who must wait. Sforno reads 'remain a widow' as 'wait', comparing Hos 3:3.

'Lest he die.' The particle expresses fear, not certainty. Rashi reads the clause as a presumption (Ketubot 43) and Judah's deferral as putting her off; Ramban rejects that, taking Judah to wait because Shelah was still a boy.

verses.translation_literal: And the days increased, and the daughter of Shua, the wife of Judah, died. And Judah was comforted, and he went up to the shearers of his flock, he and Hirah his friend the Adullamite, to Timnah.
verses.translation_dramatic: The days piled up, one upon another, and the daughter of Shua, Judah's wife, died. When the mourning had run its course, Judah was comforted. He went up to Timnah, to the shearers of his flock, he and Hirah his friend, the man of Adullam.
verses.directors_commentary: 'The days increased' is how the Hebrew compresses years; Judah's wife is again 'the daughter of Shua,' identified only through her father, and the narrator gives her one verb, died. 'He was comforted' (וַיִּנָּחֶם) names the end of mourning, which is exactly why he is free to travel. Sforno notes what is missing: with his wife gone, Judah could have brought Tamar into his house, as Isaac brought Rebekah into his mother's tent; so Tamar can read his silence as the end of any hope. Sheepshearing was the harvest of a pastoral year, and Ramban records that it was a feast with gathered company. The KJV 'sheepshearers' is correct; its 'in process of time' is a courteous way of saying that years have passed and the reader should feel them. 'Went up' (וַיַּעַל): Timnah is in the hill country, and Radak notes that Samson, coming from the other side, 'went down' to the same town. The real turn is at the end of the verse: Judah's friend Hirah is back, and the road to Timnah is the road Tamar will meet him on.

philological_notes.note: 'And he was comforted': the mourning period is over. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'after he received consolation.'
'To the shearers of his flock.' The preposition 'al' stands for 'el' (to), as in 1 Sam 1:11, according to Radak and Ibn Ezra.

verses.translation_literal: And it was told to Tamar, saying: Behold, your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his flock.
verses.translation_dramatic: The news found Tamar the way news always finds the waiting. Someone said it quietly, almost in passing: your husband's father is going up to Timnah. It is shearing time. He is going up to his flock.
verses.directors_commentary: Tamar has been sitting in her father's house, a widow twice over, while Judah's promise that Shelah would be given 'when he grows up' went stale. Notice that the narrator gives us no motive; we get only the report and the verb: it was told. Sheep-shearing was a festival of surplus and open-handedness in the ancient Near East (compare 1 Sam 25:4-8, 2 Sam 13:23-28): money flowing, wine flowing, men away from their households and loosened in their habits. The audience would hear the season as a hint. The KJV 'goeth up' is right and worth keeping: Timnah sits in the hill country, so one always goes up to it (Rashi on 38:13 makes this point by contrast with Judg 14:1, where Samson goes down). 'Thy father in law' is KJV's tidy rendering of חמיך, a word that is blunter and more intimate in Hebrew: 'your in-law' as an older man of the family who controls her fate. Say the line as a calculation, not as gossip.

philological_notes.note: 'To shear'. The verb is used for fleece-cutting; shearing time is a seasonal gathering with feasting, which sets up Judah's availability in the next verses.
'Going up': Timnah lies on higher ground. Rashi contrasts Samson's 'going down' to the same Timnah-region, which points to the approach path, not to Judah's status.

verses.translation_literal: And she removed the garments of her widowhood from upon her, and she covered with the veil, and she wrapped herself up, and she sat at the opening of Enaim, which is on the road to Timnah, for she had seen that Shelah had grown up, and she had not been given to him as a wife.
verses.translation_dramatic: She did not hesitate. The dark cloth of her widowhood came off her shoulders and lay where it fell. She took up the veil and drew it over herself, wound it close, and walked out to Enaim, where the road splits toward Timnah, and there she sat down. She had counted the years. Shelah was a grown man now, and she had not been given to him.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hinge of the chapter, and every verb belongs to Tamar. She *removes* (the same verb root as 'turn aside') the garments of widowhood, and Hebrew makes them a uniform: widow's clothes announced a woman's status and her claim on a levirate husband. Taking them off is a deliberate legal gesture as well as a disguise. The KJV's 'sat in an open place' is a guess that turns a place name into a description; the Hebrew says 'at the opening (petach) of Enaim', and 'Enaim' itself means 'two eyes' or 'springs', so there is a pun on opening and eyes that no English version carries. Rashi and Sforno think of a crossroads, where the road branches; Ibn Ezra and the STEPBible tradition take it as a village name. Either way she chooses the spot Judah must pass on his way home. 'Wrapped herself' (vatit'alaf) is a rare verb: concealment, not ornament (compare Jonah 4:8). The reason clause is the quiet bomb: 'for she saw that Shelah had grown, and she was not given to him', the story's complaint in one line. Tamar's motive is justice, not lust, and the narrator makes us see it before Judah can.

philological_notes.note: 'At the opening of Enaim.' Either a village name (Enaim, 'two springs') or, as Rashi and Rashbam read it, 'the opening of the eyes', a junction in full view of travellers. The KJV's 'open place' commits to the second reading without saying so.
'She wrapped herself up', a reflexive verb of covering; Ibn Ezra compares Jonah 4:8, Radak thinks of fine clothing. Context favours concealment of the face.
'The veil', with the definite article: a particular, known piece of clothing. Used again only of Rebekah's veil (Gen 24:65) in the Torah.

verses.translation_literal: And Judah saw her, and he considered her a prostitute, for she had covered her face.
verses.translation_dramatic: Judah came down the road and saw her, a woman alone at the crossing with her face hidden. He took her for a prostitute. A veiled face, a lone woman: that was all the evidence he needed.
verses.directors_commentary: The verbs are Judah's now, and the verdict is his: 'he considered her'. Hebrew gives the reason in a clause that cuts two ways: 'for she had covered her face'. The ancient reader supplies two thoughts at once. Rashi says it was because she sat at a crossroads; the rabbis add that in Judah's house she had always been veiled out of modesty, so he never knew her face (Rashi, Radak). Ramban prefers the plain sense, that veiled women at crossroads were understood to be soliciting. The KJV 'harlot' is archaic but the word is right: zonah is the ordinary word, with no cult attached. Mark how much the English 'thought her to be' makes it sound like a mistake of identity; the Hebrew 'considered, reckoned' (the verb of accounting) is colder: Judah *calculated* her. He assumes a role from a costume, which is the very mistake the chapter will punish.

philological_notes.note: 'And he reckoned her', a verb of accounting and assessment, not mere perception. The same verb in Gen 15:6 ('reckoned it to him as righteousness') shows how weighty a 'reckoning' can be.
The ordinary word for a prostitute; it is not the cultic term qedeshah, which Hirah will use in 38:21.

verses.translation_literal: And he turned aside to her toward the road, and he said: Come, please, let me come into you, for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. And she said: What will you give me, that you may come into me?
verses.translation_dramatic: He left the road for her. Without a name, without a look beneath the veil, he said, Come now, let me lie with you. He did not know. She was his son's widow. And she answered, quick and level: What will you give me, if you come in to me?
verses.directors_commentary: The narrator steps between the lines to tell us what Judah does not know: 'for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law'. That parenthesis is the whole irony, and the KJV's brackets get it right. The verb is 'come into' (bo' el), which repeats in her answer, so Hebrew makes him say it and she say it back to him word for word, turning his request into a bargain. The KJV 'Go to' for הבה is archaic: hava is the same word as 'Come, let us build a city' (Gen 11:4), a summons to act, so 'Come now' is the force. Her 'What will you give me' is the price question every client would hear, but see Sforno: she is steering him to make an offer, so that there will be a pledge. Price talk in an ancient Near Eastern encounter of this kind was ordinary; a payment in kind such as a kid was standard.

philological_notes.note: 'Come now', an imperative that urges action, not 'give'. The same form summons the builders of Babel (Gen 11:4). The KJV's 'Go to' is an archaism for the same sense.
'Let me come into you', the plain idiom of intercourse, and the same phrase returns in her mouth in the same verse.

verses.translation_literal: And he said: I will send a kid of the goats from the flock. And she said: If you give a pledge until your sending [it].
verses.translation_dramatic: I will send you a young goat from my flock, he said. A kid. And she did not take his word. A pledge, then, she said, something in my hand until it comes.
verses.directors_commentary: A kid of the goats was the ordinary payment, and the pledge ('erabon') the ordinary guarantee: a sheep-owner's promise had no force without a deposit, and Judah is away from his flock. The KJV's 'Wilt thou give me a pledge' turns her half-sentence into a question; Hebrew leaves it as an unfinished 'if you give a pledge until you send', which makes her sound like she is thinking aloud, setting terms. Two details pay off later. The word 'kid of the goats' is the same animal Judah and his brothers once used to deceive Jacob (Gen 37:31), and the rabbis do not miss the irony (Rashi on 38:23, citing Genesis Rabbah). 'Sending' (shalach) is a keyword of the story, running through the next verses. Rashbam notes that 'until your sending' also covers sending a gift by a messenger, which is exactly what Judah will do.

philological_notes.note: 'A pledge', a deposit held as security (Rashi: mashkon). The word occurs only here and in vv. 18, 20 in the Bible. It later gives Greek-via-Hebrew 'arrabon' in the New Testament.

verses.translation_literal: And he said: What is the pledge that I shall give you? And she said: Your seal, and your cord, and your staff which is in your hand. And he gave to her, and he came into her, and she conceived by him.
verses.translation_dramatic: What pledge, then? he asked. Your seal, she said, and your cord, and the staff in your hand. She named the three things that were Judah himself. He gave them to her. He went in to her, and she conceived.
verses.directors_commentary: She asks for the three objects that identify a man of standing without a name: the cylinder or stamp seal that signs his contracts, the cord on which it hung round his neck, and his staff, which in the ancient Near East was a personal emblem carved or marked to the owner. Each is legally a signature. The KJV 'bracelets' is wrong: petilekha is 'your cord', and singular (the plural 'cords' only appears in 38:25 for the set). Ramban objects to Rashi's 'garment' on exactly these grounds. The STEPBible gloss 'seal' and the ASV 'signet' are right. Notice the speed of the last verbs: he gave, he came in, she conceived: four short clauses and a pregnancy, the way Hebrew narrative dispatches an event it does not wish to dwell on. 'Conceived to him' (lo) carries a faint legal sense: by him, for him, in his line.

philological_notes.note: 'Your seal': the cylinder or stamp seal, the owner's signature. Rashi renders it 'ring'; Radak adds 'with which one seals'.
'Your cord', the string on which the seal hung. Rashi reads 'garment', Rashbam 'belt', Radak 'garment or head-cloth'; Ramban rejects 'garment'. The KJV 'bracelets' has no support in the Hebrew.
'And she conceived to him.' The 'to him' marks the child as his: the standard idiom for a conception in a man's line.

verses.translation_literal: And she arose, and she went, and she removed her veil from upon her, and she put on the garments of her widowhood.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then she rose and went. Somewhere out of sight the veil came off, and the dark cloth of her widowhood went back on, as though nothing had happened at all.
verses.directors_commentary: Four verbs in a row, all hers: arose, went, removed, put on. The verse is the mirror of 38:14, where the same verbs ran in reverse, and the repetition shuts the scene like a lid. Radak and Sforno take the return to widow's clothes as proof that her aim was never a husband or pleasure, only offspring from Judah's line, and now that she has what she came for she resumes her station. The KJV 'laid by' for 'removed' is fine but archaic. Note too that the veil is now 'her veil', no longer 'the veil': it goes back to being hers, and she goes back to being herself.

philological_notes.note: 'And she put on', the exact reverse of 'she removed' in 38:14. Radak reads the act as showing she wanted only offspring.

verses.translation_literal: And Judah sent the kid of the goats by the hand of his friend the Adullamite, to take the pledge from the hand of the woman, and he did not find her.
verses.translation_dramatic: Judah kept his word. He sent the kid by the hand of his friend, the man of Adullam, and told him to bring back the pledge from the woman's hand. The man came to the place. He did not find her.
verses.directors_commentary: Judah does what an honourable man does: pays the debt and redeems the pledge. The Hebrew says 'by the hand of his friend' and 'from the hand of the woman': hand to hand, a transaction. The KJV matches the Hebrew here and the BBE inserts 'Hirah', which is not in this verse (we know him from 38:12). The one flat 'and he did not find her' is the whole scene: the speaker who thought he had bought something finds only an empty road. Notice that the woman is 'the woman' (ha-ishah), not 'the harlot'. The narrator has not once called Tamar a prostitute in his own voice. A friend is sent because a man of Judah's standing does not go back himself to a roadside place.

philological_notes.note: 'His friend the Adullamite' (Hirah, named in 38:1, 12). The word for friend, re'a, is the companion of equals.

verses.translation_literal: And he asked the men of her place, saying: Where is the consecrated woman, she at Enaim, on the road? And they said: There has not been in this place a consecrated woman.
verses.translation_dramatic: He asked the men of the place, politely, with a lowered voice: Where is the holy woman, the one who sat at Enaim by the road? And they looked at him as if he had asked after a ghost. There has never been a holy woman here, they said.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the vocabulary shifts, and the KJV does not tell you. Judah called her a zonah in 38:15; Hirah, asking the locals, uses qedeshah, literally 'a consecrated woman' (from the root of 'holy'). The word is a euphemism, and a courteous one: the friend of a man of rank does not ask a village for 'the whore'. Whether qedeshah means a cult prostitute attached to a shrine is debated; Rashi and Rashbam read it as a woman set apart for anyone who comes. Either way, the KJV's 'harlot' hides that the text has changed registers, and that the men's blank answer is unanswerable: 'there has been no qedeshah here'. Their reply is exactly true, since there was no sacred woman at all, only a widow in a veil. 'Her place' (meqomah) can also mean 'the men of her locality'.

philological_notes.note: 'Consecrated woman': the word for a woman designated for sexual service, often with a cultic connotation, in a respectable register compared with zonah. Whether temple prostitution is meant is disputed; Rashi reads it as 'set apart and prepared for the act'.
'The men of her place': the locals of the area where she sat. Radak reads 'the lane (mavoi) she lived in'.

verses.translation_literal: And he returned to Judah, and he said: I did not find her, and also the men of the place said: There has not been in this place a consecrated woman.
verses.translation_dramatic: So he went back to Judah with the kid still at his side. I did not find her, he said. And the men of the place said the same: there has never been such a woman here.
verses.directors_commentary: Hirah repeats the villagers' sentence almost word for word, 'there has not been in this place a qedeshah', the exact wording of the previous verse, so the report arrives intact and untouched. The KJV 'I cannot find her' softens a plain past tense: 'I did not find her'. The 'also' (gam) matters: two negatives, his own failure and the locals' denial, stack up like proof. Sforno hears mockery in the men's answer, as if they are laughing at Judah's expense; the text does not say so, but a good actor can play the line with that edge.

philological_notes.note: 'And also': the second witness. Sforno reads the men's answer as mockery of Judah's honour.

verses.translation_literal: And Judah said: Let her take for herself, lest we become a contempt. Behold, I sent this kid, and you did not find her.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let her keep them, Judah said. Let her have the things. If we go on asking, we become the story of the road. Look, I sent the kid. You could not find her. That is the end of it.
verses.directors_commentary: Judah closes the matter in four short statements and a worry about shame. 'Lest we become a contempt' (pen nihyeh lavuz): the Hebrew puts him and Hirah together as one reputation, and 'bûz' is the word for public disdain. The KJV 'lest we be shamed' is close; the subject is the shame of a man who would be laughed at for chasing a prostitute, not guilt over the act. He is not troubled by the pledge itself: he gave three personal items, which no one lightly leaves behind, and he abandons them without a second thought, which tells the audience how much he thought of the encounter. Rashi hears the irony the rabbis hear: Judah, who deceived his father with a goat's blood, has now been deceived with a goat (Genesis Rabbah, cited by Rashi). The line 'I sent this kid' is his alibi: he kept his word, and says so twice.

philological_notes.note: 'Contempt, scorn': public disdain, a social disgrace. Rashi and Radak read the fear as being a laughing-stock if the affair is publicised.
'Let her take for herself': let her keep what she holds. Rashbam: the sense is 'what is in her hand'; Ibn Ezra: leave it with her.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, about three months, and it was told to Judah, saying: Tamar your daughter-in-law has committed prostitution, and also, behold, she is pregnant by prostitution. And Judah said: Bring her out, and let her be burned.
verses.translation_dramatic: Three months went by, or near enough. And then word was brought to Judah: Tamar, your son's widow, has played the harlot. And more than that: she is with child by it. And Judah, with no pause, no question, said: Bring her out, and let her be burned.
verses.directors_commentary: 'About three months': the time a pregnancy first shows. The rabbis take it as the whole of the middle month plus parts of the first and last (Genesis Rabbah 85, in Rashi and Radak). The report to Judah is built in two stages: 'she has acted the prostitute' and 'moreover, she is pregnant by prostitution', so the accusation arrives with the evidence. Judah's sentence is instant and pronounced as head of the clan: 'bring her out' and let her be burned. The KJV 'let her be burnt' is accurate, and 'bring her forth' is fine. The legal logic, as Radak and Rashbam explain, is that a widow promised to a brother-in-law (the shomeret yavam) is treated as another man's wife, and Judah is the one with authority over her. Ramban finds the rabbinic account of her as a priest's daughter unconvincing and proposes Judah as a ruler passing sentence in his own right. Whatever the rule, the irony is complete: the man who 'considered her a prostitute' on a roadside now condemns the same word in her. 'Prostitution' appears twice in the report (zanta, zenunim), the same root that was the whole of his sin on the road.

philological_notes.note: 'Has acted as a prostitute': a verb of illicit sexual conduct; it is the same root as zonah in 38:15, so the charge uses the word that Judah himself applied to her.
'By prostitution': a plural noun of the same root. Rashi: 'she is pregnant by fornication' in the fashion of 'a pregnant woman'.

'Let her be burned': a jussive that is a verdict. Rashi cites a tradition that she was a priest's daughter; Radak and Rashbam ground it in her status as promised to Shelah; Ramban doubts the rabbinic reasoning.

verses.translation_literal: She [was] being brought out, and she, she sent to her father-in-law, saying, “To the man whose these [are], I [am] pregnant.” And she said, “Recognize, please, whose [are] the seal and the cords and the staff, these.”
verses.translation_dramatic: They were already bringing her out. And still she was not done. She sent a word ahead of her to her father-in-law, and the word was careful, and it named no one: “By the man who owns these, I am with child.” Then, as the silence stretched, she added the one thing that could not be argued with: “Look closely. Whose are they? This seal, these cords, this staff.”
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene turns on one participle. Tamar is *being brought out* to the fire Judah ordered in v24, and from that spot she sends the proof she had kept. She does not say “you.” She says “the man whose these are,” and lets him reach the conclusion himself. Rashi, Radak and Sforno all notice this and read it as mercy: she would rather burn than shame him in public. Play it as someone with nothing left to lose who still will not strike first.

The objects are the identity papers of the age. The seal (חֹתֶמֶת) was a personal stamp used to sign and close documents; the cord (פָּתִיל) is the string it hung from, and the staff (מַטֶּה) was a man’s walking stick, often carved so that it could be told from every other. Together they are Judah’s signature, his ID and his walking-stick, and no one in the camp could mistake them. The KJV’s “signet, and bracelets” is wrong on the second item: פְּתִילִים are cords or threads, not jewellery. The KJV also writes “By the man, whose these are, am I with child,” which keeps the Hebrew order but sounds like a riddle; the Hebrew is blunt and unadorned.

The key word is הַכֶּר־נָא, “recognize, please.” It is the same verb the brothers used when they brought Joseph’s bloodied coat to Jacob (37:32, הַכֶּר־נָא הַכְּתֹנֶת בִּנְךָ הִוא). Judah deceived his father with an object and a demand to identify it; now the same demand comes back to him. Genesis Rabbah, cited by Radak, says it outright: “you said to your father ‘recognize,’ and now Tamar says ‘recognize’ to you.” The story is built so the listener hears it.

philological_notes.note: ‘Recognize, please.’ The verb is the very one in 37:32 where Judah’s brothers presented Joseph’s coat; the echo is deliberate irony. נָא softens the command into a request.
The seal or signet, here a personal item that marks ownership and authenticates a document. It is the object of the pledge made in v18.
Passive participle: she is being brought out. Ibn Ezra notes it is an unusual form, with its aleph kept.

verses.translation_literal: And Judah recognized, and he said, “She is in the right, more than I, because on this account I did not give her to Shelah my son.” And he did not add again to know her.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Judah looked, and knew them. They were his. For a long breath he said nothing; then he said it, plainly, in front of them all: “She is more in the right than I am. I never gave her to my son Shelah.” He did not go to her again.
verses.directors_commentary:
The man who ordered a woman burned for something he himself had done now speaks the shortest confession in Genesis. He does not defend himself and does not plead. The verb וַיַּכֵּר, “he recognized,” answers Tamar’s הַכֶּר־נָא in the previous verse; he does what she asked and no more.

צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי is usually “she is more righteous than I.” The KJV’s “righteous” sounds like a moral grade; צדק is a legal word, to be in the right, to have the stronger case. Rashbam, Ramban and Radak all read the min as comparative, with parallels in 1 Sam 24:18 and 1 Kgs 2:32. Rashi offers the other reading: “from me [she is pregnant].” Rabbinic tradition (Sotah 10b) hears a voice from heaven confirm that, but the plain sense is a man naming his own debt. The debt is Shelah: by the custom of levirate marriage (Gen 38:8), the surviving brother raises a child for the dead one, and Judah withheld Shelah, keeping his one remaining son out of reach.

The last clause is a euphemism the KJV carries well: “he knew her again no more.” לדעתה means sexual relations, and וְלֹא־יָסַף, “did not add,” closes the line. Rashi and Ramban record a dispute whether יסף here means “did not do it again” or “did not stop”; the plain sense is the first. Radak’s reading is that he saw the first union as a sin of contempt, since he had thought her a prostitute.

philological_notes.note: ‘She is in the right, more than I.’ The min is comparative, as in 1 Sam 24:18, where Saul says the same of David. The Hebrew carries a legal sense: she has the better case.
‘To know her’: the usual euphemism for sexual relations, kept in the literal layer.
‘He added.’ Rashi and Ramban record the alternative ‘did not cease’ against the plain ‘did not repeat.’

verses.translation_literal: And it was at the time of her giving birth, and look, twins in her womb.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the day came when she was to give birth. And there, in the womb, was not one child but two.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tempo changes with a single word. הִנֵּה, “look!”, is the midwife’s surprise, put into the narration as though the listener were standing in the room. The text has said nothing of twins until this moment. Radak takes it that Tamar felt only one child until the birth; Sforno, that the twins were known before it. The narration lets the listener learn it at the labour.

The KJV’s “travail” is accurate in the old sense, labour pains, but the Hebrew is flat: *at the time of her giving birth*. The word for twins is תְאוֹמִים, written here with the vowel letter, and Rashi and Radak (taking it from the rabbis) contrast it with Rebekah’s twins in Gen 25:24, where the same word is written short, תוֹמִם, as the one of them was wicked. That is a rabbinic lesson drawn from spelling; the plain point is that the story of Isaac’s sons is being replayed with a new set of brothers.

For the audience, the echo matters: Jacob and Esau fought in the womb over who would lead. Here the same fight is about to be fought at the door.

philological_notes.note: ‘Twins.’ Written in full here against the short spelling in Gen 25:24; Rashi and Radak build a lesson on the difference, which the plain text does not need.

verses.translation_literal: And it was in her giving birth, and he gave a hand, and the midwife took, and she tied on his hand a scarlet thread, saying, “This one came out first.”
verses.translation_dramatic: And in the labour, one of them thrust out a hand. The midwife was quick: she took it, and round the small wrist she wound a scarlet thread. “This one,” she said, “came out first.”
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene is a delivery room, and the midwife is the only person who acts; the mother says nothing. The child “gave a hand,” וַיִּתֶּן יָד: the idiom is literal and a little comic, as though the baby were extending a hand to be shaken. The midwife’s thread is a practical mark. In a world of inheritance rights, the firstborn’s share and standing depended on who came out first, and a midwife who could not say would leave the family without an answer. The thread is שָׁנִי, scarlet or crimson, a dye made from the scale insect *Kermes*; it was costly and bright, and visible at once.

The KJV’s “bound upon his hand” is fair. The BBE’s “red thread” is accurate but loses the sense of an expensive dye. Ibn Ezra and Radak note that the baby’s hand went back in; the tie was a record of an event that was about to be overturned. That is the point: the midwife declares a firstborn before the birth is finished, and the verse sets her up to be wrong.

philological_notes.note: Scarlet or crimson, a dyed thread; the colour of a costly dye, here visible and unmistakable.
‘The midwife’, a piel participle, literally ‘the one who causes to give birth.’

verses.translation_literal: And it was, as he was drawing back his hand, and behold, his brother came out; and she said, What! You have breached upon yourself a breach! And someone called his name Perez.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the hand slipped back, drawn in like something pulled from the light. And then, there: his brother, out, all at once, in a rush and a cry. The midwife stared at the small, furious body. “What a breach,” she said. “What a breach you have burst through — and upon your own head!” And the child was named for it: Perez, the Breaker.
verses.directors_commentary:
The midwife has just tied a scarlet thread on the hand that came out first (v. 28), and now the claim collapses: the hand retreats and the other twin shoves past it. In a world where the firstborn takes the double share and the headship of the house, who comes out first is not trivia but inheritance, and Judah's line has already lost two firstborn sons in this chapter. Her cry is half astonishment, half reproach, the voice of a professional watching a birth go sideways.

The Hebrew plays on one root: 'you have breached (paratzta) a breach (paretz)', then the name Perez. The KJV, 'How hast thou broken forth? this breach be upon thee', turns an exclamation into a question, adds a wish ('be upon thee') the Hebrew does not state, and by switching between 'broken forth' and 'breach' loses the sound-link between the cry and the name. The ASV's 'for thyself' is closer in sense but also drops the repeated root. 'Upon you' (עליך) is itself disputed: Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as a liability resting on the child, Rashi and Ramban as a breach made against himself, as through a fence that enclosed him. The KJV's 'therefore' is also an addition: Hebrew has a plain 'and he called', and Radak says it was Judah. Perez means 'breach, bursting through'; for the later reader he is the ancestor of David (Ruth 4:18-22).

philological_notes.note: To breach or burst through, as of a wall or fence. The midwife applies the language of a broken barrier to a birth; the same root gives the noun פֶּרֶץ and the name. Ramban notes the root can be used of crossing any boundary (Gen 28:14, 30:43).
Literally 'upon you'. Read either as a breach made upon yourself (Rashi, Ramban) or a consequence resting on you (Ibn Ezra, Radak). The literal layer keeps 'upon yourself'.

verses.translation_literal: And afterward his brother came out, the one on whose hand [was] the scarlet thread, and someone called his name Zerah.
verses.translation_dramatic: And afterward his brother came out, the one with the scarlet thread still bound about his hand. And he was named Zerah, the Dawn-Red.
verses.directors_commentary:
The story ends with a quiet reversal. The thread meant to mark the firstborn now marks the second. The Hebrew does not say who is the legal firstborn; it says only that Perez came out first and Zerah afterward, and that the thread went with the child who did not lead. In a society where the first out of the womb carried the family’s weight, the midwife’s knot has proved useless.

The name זֶרַח comes from a root meaning to rise or shine, as the sun does; Rashi and Radak connect it to the scarlet thread, and Rashbam to the reddening of dawn. The Hebrew gives no reason at all, unlike Perez’s name in v29, and so the explanation is the rabbis’, not the text’s. The KJV’s “Zarah” reflects the old spelling; the Hebrew is the same name as Zerah of Joshua 7, where Achan, “son of Zerah,” takes the devoted things. Rashi’s Genesis Rabbah note counts four mentions of “hand” in the passage against Achan’s four forbidden items, which is an inference of the rabbis and not a claim of the text.

The author leaves both brothers’ futures to the genealogies: Perez is the line to David (Ruth 4:18–22), and Zerah’s line is recorded separately in 1 Chr 2:6.

philological_notes.note: The name means ‘rising’ or ‘shining’, as of the sun. Rashi and Radak tie it to the brightness of the scarlet thread; Rashbam reads it as redness. The text itself gives no reason.

events.title: Judah leaves his brothers and lodges with Hirah of Adullam
events.narrative_summary: At that time Judah goes down from his brothers and turns aside to an Adullamite named Hirah.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'At that time' (v1) ties the chapter to the sale of Joseph. Radak and the midrash read it as after the sale; Ibn Ezra reads it as shortly before it. Anchored on the end of Jacob's mourning (jacob_mourns), with no offset and a margin of 2 years to cover both readings. Hebron to Adullam is about 21 km by road, 5.5 hours on foot (urim travel); 6 hours.

events.title: Judah takes the daughter of Shua as his wife
events.narrative_summary: Judah sees the daughter of a Canaanite named Shua, marries her and has relations with her.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No time word. He sees her 'there', so the marriage follows some time in Adullam; 3 months with a margin of 3 months. It takes the tier of 'at that time' (MACRO_ERA).

events.title: Judah's wife bears Er
events.narrative_summary: She conceives and bears a son, and Judah names him Er.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Gestation of about 9 months after the marriage; no time word, so MACRO_ERA like the scene it belongs to.

events.title: She bears a second son, Onan
events.narrative_summary: She conceives again and bears a son, whom she names Onan.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'Again' only gives order. About a year after Er, with a margin of 6 months.

events.title: She bears a third son, Shelah, at Chezib
events.narrative_summary: She bears yet another son, calls him Shelah, and Judah is at Chezib when she bears him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: About a year after Onan, margin 6 months. Chezib is Achzib (loc.achzib), 5 km from Adullam by the packet's coordinates; the move is not dated. In v5 the subject of 'he was' is ambiguous (Judah or Shelah).

events.title: Judah takes Tamar as a wife for Er
events.narrative_summary: Judah takes a wife named Tamar for his firstborn Er.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The text gives no age. A boy of about 13 marries; the margin is 3 years. This leaves Shelah old enough by v14 and keeps the story near the 22 years from Joseph's sale to the descent into Egypt (Ibn Ezra on v1 raises that squeeze).

events.title: Er is wicked and the LORD puts him to death
events.narrative_summary: Er, Judah's firstborn, is evil in the LORD's eyes, and the LORD kills him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No time given; Tamar has borne no child, so a short marriage: 1 year with a margin of 1 year. Pseudo-Jonathan says Er avoided giving her seed.

events.title: Judah tells Onan to raise up seed for his brother
events.narrative_summary: Judah tells Onan to go in to his brother's wife, act as a brother-in-law and raise up offspring for his brother.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: After the mourning for Er, so about a month with a margin of a month.

events.title: Onan spills his seed on the ground
events.narrative_summary: Onan knows the offspring will not be his, and whenever he goes in to his brother's wife he spoils it on the ground so as not to give seed to his brother.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A repeated act ('whenever he went in'), starting some months after the order; 3 months with a margin of 3 months.

events.title: The LORD puts Onan to death as well
events.narrative_summary: What Onan did is evil in the LORD's eyes, and he kills him too.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No interval in the text; a month with a margin of a month after the repeated act.

events.title: Judah sends Tamar home to wait for Shelah
events.narrative_summary: Judah tells Tamar to stay a widow in her father's house until his son Shelah grows up, for he fears Shelah too will die. Tamar goes and lives there.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: After the mourning for Onan; a month with a margin of a month. Shelah is still a boy: born about 3 years after Er.

events.title: Judah and Hirah go up to Timnah for the sheepshearing
events.narrative_summary: Judah, with his friend Hirah the Adullamite, goes up to Timnah to his sheepshearers.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Shearing is a spring season, a month after the comfort with a margin of a month. Judah sets out from Adullam toward Timnah; the duration is the first leg to Enaim (5 km by road, 1.5 hours on foot, urim travel). The rest of the road, Enaim to Timnah, is about 4.5 hours more.

events.title: Shua's daughter dies and Judah is comforted
events.narrative_summary: The days multiply, Judah's wife dies, and Judah is comforted after mourning.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'The days were multiplied' (v12) is vague. Long enough for Shelah to grow (v14); about 2 years with a margin of 1 year puts him at about 15. The 1-month duration covers death and comfort.

events.title: Tamar, told of Judah's trip, veils herself at Enaim
events.narrative_summary: Tamar is told that her father-in-law is going up to Timnah. She takes off her widow's clothes, veils herself and sits at the entrance of Enaim on the road to Timnah, because Shelah has grown and she has not been given to him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: She hears when Judah sets out and takes her seat before he arrives: the same start as his departure, lasting as long as his first leg. Her home's distance from Enaim is not given; margin 2 hours.

events.title: Judah mistakes the veiled Tamar for a prostitute and proposes
events.narrative_summary: Judah sees her, thinks her a prostitute because she has covered her face, and turns aside to ask to go in to her. She asks what he will give her.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Continuous with her taking the seat; he reaches Enaim as she sits.

events.title: Judah leaves his seal, cord and staff as a pledge and lies with her
events.narrative_summary: He promises a kid from the flock. She asks for a pledge: his seal, cord and staff. He gives them, goes in to her, and she conceives.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Continuous bargaining; a couple of hours. Conception here dates the later three-month report and the birth.

events.title: Tamar goes and puts her widow's clothes back on
events.narrative_summary: She rises, goes, takes off her veil and puts on her widow's clothes.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Right after he leaves.

events.title: Judah sends the kid by Hirah to recover the pledge
events.narrative_summary: Judah sends the kid by his friend Hirah to take back the pledge, but Hirah does not find the woman.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: He sends it after the shearing business at Timnah; 3 days after the encounter with a margin of 2 days. The duration is the walk back from Timnah to Enaim with a kid (about 18 km, 4.5 hours, urim travel, walk).

events.title: Hirah asks the men of Enaim and returns without her
events.narrative_summary: Hirah asks the men of the place where the cult prostitute at Enaim on the road is, and they say there has been none there. He returns to Judah and says he has not found her.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Asking at Enaim, then the walk to Timnah (4.5 hours, urim travel). About 5 hours with a margin of 3.

events.title: Judah says to let her keep the pledge
events.narrative_summary: Judah says to let her keep it, lest they be shamed, since he sent the kid and Hirah did not find her.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Immediately on Hirah's report.

events.title: Judah is told Tamar is pregnant and orders her burned
events.narrative_summary: About three months later Judah is told that Tamar has played the prostitute and is with child. He says to bring her out and burn her.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'About three months' (v24) from the conception, with a margin of 3 weeks. Rashi, citing Niddah, says it counts the greater part of the first and last month with the whole middle, i.e. just over two months; I keep three with a margin that reaches it. Anchored on the union, not on Hirah's search.

events.title: Tamar sends Judah the seal, cord and staff
events.narrative_summary: As she is brought out, she sends to her father-in-law: 'By the man to whom these belong I am with child.' She asks him to identify the seal, the cords and the staff.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: While she is being brought out, so within hours. Pseudo-Jonathan adds her prayer.

events.title: Judah acknowledges the pledge and says she is more righteous
events.narrative_summary: Judah recognizes them and says she is more righteous than he, since he did not give her to Shelah. He does not know her again.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Immediately on seeing the objects.

events.title: Tamar goes into labour with twins
events.narrative_summary: When she comes to give birth, there are twins in her womb.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Nine months of pregnancy from the conception at the union; twins often come early, so a margin of a month. The labour is taken as 12 hours. The verse does not say how long after the verdict; about 6 months after v26 given v24 'three months'.

events.title: A hand comes out and the midwife ties a scarlet thread on it
events.narrative_summary: One twin puts out a hand, and the midwife ties a scarlet thread on it, saying this one came out first.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A beat inside the labour, with a margin of 6 hours.

events.title: The hand withdraws and Perez comes out first
events.narrative_summary: As he draws back his hand, his brother comes out. She says 'what a breach you have made', and he is called Perez.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Directly after the hand is withdrawn.

events.title: The brother with the scarlet thread is born and called Zerah
events.narrative_summary: Afterwards his brother, with the scarlet thread on his hand, comes out and is called Zerah.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'Afterward' (v30) after Perez.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Because Er dies childless, Judah commands Onan to raise up seed for him (v8).
Tamar is told that her father-in-law is going up to Timnah, and she sits veiled on that road (v13-14).
Judah withheld Shelah, and Tamar sees that he is grown yet she was not given to him (v11, v14).
After two sons die, Judah fears Shelah will die too and keeps him from Tamar (v11).
What Onan did was evil in the LORD's eyes, and so the LORD put him to death (v10).
Judah promised a kid and left a pledge, so he sends the kid to redeem it (v17, v20).
The seal, cord and staff she took as a pledge are the proof she sends (v18, v25).
She conceives by Judah (v18) and the twins are born (v27-30).
Being brought out to be burned, she sends the pledge to Judah (v24-25).
Judah recognizes the objects she sends and confesses (v25-26).

entities.etymology_meaning: A stamp seal, the cord it hangs from, and a staff — personal marks of identity.
entities.summary_bio: The three identifying items Judah gives Tamar as pledge for the promised kid. Tamar keeps them and later produces them to prove the father of her child.

entities.etymology_meaning: A young goat from the flock, the promised payment.
entities.summary_bio: The payment Judah promises the veiled woman. He sends it by Hirah, who cannot find her to deliver it.
The residents of Enaim whom Hirah asks about the 'cult prostitute'. They answer that none has been there.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'deceitful' or 'a lie' (a place of failing springs).
entities.summary_bio: A town in Judah's lowland where Shelah is born. It is probably the later Achzib of Joshua 15:44 and Micah 1:14.

entities.etymology_meaning: Meaning uncertain; perhaps 'refuge' or 'sealed off place'.
entities.summary_bio: A Canaanite town in the Judean lowland (Shephelah), home of Hirah. Judah settles near it after leaving his brothers.

entities.etymology_meaning: 'Two springs' or 'eyes'; the text may also read 'at the opening of the eyes' (an open place).
entities.summary_bio: A place on the road to Timnah where Tamar sits veiled. The men there deny any cult prostitute ever stood by the road.
A town in the hill country of Judah where Judah goes up to shear his sheep. Tamar sits on the road leading to it.

entities.etymology_meaning: Unnamed; identified only by her father.
entities.summary_bio: A Canaanite woman whom Judah takes as wife. She bears Er, Onan and Shelah and dies after the days multiply.
Judah's firstborn, married to Tamar. He is evil in the LORD's eyes and the LORD puts him to death, leaving Tamar childless.
An Adullamite, Judah's friend and host after Judah leaves his brothers. He accompanies Judah to the sheepshearing at Timnah and carries the kid to redeem Judah's pledge.
The midwife who attends Tamar's labour. She ties a scarlet thread on the first hand to appear and remarks on the second twin's breach.
Judah's second son. Charged to raise up offspring for Er with Tamar, he deliberately prevents conception to keep the heirship from Er, and the LORD puts him to death.

entities.etymology_meaning: 'Breach' or 'breaking through', from the midwife's cry at his birth.
entities.summary_bio: Twin son of Judah and Tamar, who breaks through ahead of his brother. He is the ancestor of the line of David.
Judah's third son, born at Chezib. Judah withholds him from Tamar for fear he will die, though he grows up.
A Canaanite man whose daughter Judah marries. He appears only as her father.
Wife of Judah's firstborn Er, left a childless widow by his death and Onan's refusal. Denied Shelah, she disguises herself, conceives twins by Judah himself, and is declared more righteous than he.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'rising' or 'dawn', perhaps recalling the scarlet (red) thread.
entities.summary_bio: Twin son of Judah and Tamar, whose hand with the scarlet thread appeared first but who is born second.

components.evidence_explanation: GEN.38.7 says the LORD put him to death.
GEN.38.1 says Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to Hirah the Adullamite.
GEN.38.2 says he took her; GEN.38.12 says she died.
GEN.38.18 says Judah gave them to her; GEN.38.20 shows she keeps them.
GEN.38.25 says Tamar sent them to Judah to identify; GEN.38.26 says he recognised them.
GEN.38.10 says the LORD put him to death also.
GEN.38.29 says Perez came out after the hand withdrew, ahead of his brother.
GEN.38.14 says she covered herself with a veil; GEN.38.19 says she removed it.
GEN.38.11 says she went and dwelt in her father's house.
GEN.38.18 says she conceived by him; GEN.38.24 shows it is visible three months later.
GEN.38.6 says Judah took a wife for Er his firstborn.
GEN.38.7 gives Er's death; GEN.38.11 calls her to remain a widow.

components.label_value: Second to emerge, hand marked first
components.evidence_explanation: GEN.38.30 says he came out afterward, the one with the scarlet thread on his hand.

systems.name: Divine judgment by sudden death
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Sudden death was commonly read as divine punishment for offence. Here the narrator says plainly the LORD did it, and gives the reason (evil in his eyes) without describing the manner.
rules_and_mechanics: The LORD alone is the agent.
The cause is stated as wickedness or a deed evil in the LORD's eyes.
The death is immediate and without human intermediary.

systems.name: Levirate marriage (yibbum)
systems.ancient_near_east_context: A widow without a son is married to her husband's brother so the first son carries the dead man's name and inheritance. Close parallels appear in Hittite and Middle Assyrian law, and Deuteronomy 25:5–10 later codifies the Israelite form.
rules_and_mechanics: The brother of a childless dead man takes the widow.
The first son counts as the dead brother's heir.
The widow stays in the family until the duty is met.
Refusal is a breach of family duty.

systems.name: Burning as penalty for sexual offence
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Burning appears in later Israelite law for specific sexual offences (Lev 20:14; 21:9) and in some other ancient laws. Here Judah, as head of the family, orders the sentence without any court.
rules_and_mechanics: Applied to a woman bound to a household who is accused of harlotry.

systems.name: Pledge for deferred payment
systems.ancient_near_east_context: When payment could not be made at once, the debtor left an identifying object as security. Seals were personal, hung on cords, and acted as signatures; staffs often bore marks of owner or clan.
rules_and_mechanics: A debtor promises payment and leaves a pledge.
The pledge stays with the creditor until payment.
The pledge is returned when payment is made.

systems.name: Sheepshearing
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Shearing was a seasonal communal event, usually in spring, with feasting and sometimes commercial dealings. Other texts (1 Sam 25, 2 Sam 13) show it as a time of celebration and exposure.
rules_and_mechanics: Owners travel to meet the shearers.
Travellers along the road are expected.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Told Tamar is pregnant by harlotry, Judah orders her brought out to be burned.
system_instances.significance_note: It sets up Judah's unwitting self-condemnation and reversal in the next verse.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD puts Er to death because he was evil in the LORD's eyes.
system_instances.significance_note: It leaves Tamar a childless widow and sets up the duty of the next brother.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Judah tells Onan to go in to his brother's wife and raise up offspring for Er.
system_instances.significance_note: It states the custom that drives the rest of the chapter.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Onan goes in to Tamar but spills his seed on the ground so as to give no offspring to his brother.
system_instances.significance_note: Onan's refusal is a betrayal of family duty, and Tamar remains without a child.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD puts Onan to death, as with his brother.
system_instances.significance_note: Two sons dead, which turns Judah's fear onto Tamar and keeps Shelah from her.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Judah promises a kid and leaves his seal, cord and staff as pledge before lying with the veiled woman.
system_instances.significance_note: The pledge later identifies Judah as father and proves Tamar's claim.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Judah, recently comforted, goes up with Hirah to his shearers at Timnah.
system_instances.significance_note: The trip puts Judah on the road where Tamar waits.

edges.description: Judah tells Onan to marry Tamar and raise up offspring for Er.
Told that Tamar has played the harlot and is pregnant, Judah orders her burned.
Judah sends Hirah with the kid to collect his pledge from the woman.
Judah tells Tamar to live as a widow at her father's house until Shelah grows up.
Judah turns aside to the veiled woman and asks to lie with her, not knowing she is his daughter-in-law.
Judah recognises the items and says Tamar is more righteous than he, because he never gave her to Shelah.
The midwife ties a scarlet thread on the hand that came out first, so as to identify the firstborn.
Onan spills his seed on the ground so that Tamar will not conceive for Er.
Tamar sends Judah the seal, cord and staff and asks him to say whose they are.
Tamar takes off her widow's clothes and veils herself on the road so that Judah will not know her.
Tamar asks for Judah's seal, cord and staff as security for the kid he promises.
The LORD puts Er to death for being evil in his sight.
The LORD puts Onan to death for what he had done.
